items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
- Trials are most useful when attached to a decision rather than memorised as isolated acronyms.
- The studies below are grouped around three everyday questions: How should I recognise and resuscitate impaired perfusion?
- Which fluid and how much?
- Which vasopressor or haemostatic strategy is supported?
- The numbers reflect the reported study populations and endpoints, not universal expected outcomes for every surgical patient.

## 11.1 Perfusion targets, timing and individualisation

| **Trial** | **Study and principal result** | **ANZCA Final clinical interpretation** |
|---|---|---|
| [Rivers EGDT (2001)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa010307) | Single-centre ED trial of early goal-directed therapy for severe sepsis/septic shock reported lower in-hospital mortality with protocolised treatment (30.5% vs 46.5%). | Historically established early recognition and organised resuscitation, but its entire CVP/ScvO₂/transfusion/inotrope bundle should **not** be reproduced uncritically as contemporary standard care. |
| [ProCESS (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1401602) | Multicentre US RCT compared protocol-based EGDT, protocol-based standard therapy and usual care; no significant 60-day mortality difference. | Early sepsis care matters; mandatory invasive EGDT protocols add little to good contemporary resuscitation for unselected patients. |
| [ARISE (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1404380) | Australasian-led multicentre trial; EGDT did not reduce 90-day all-cause mortality compared with usual care. | A particularly relevant Australasian landmark. Do not use fixed CVP or ScvO₂ targets as proof of volume responsiveness or resuscitation adequacy. |
| [ProMISe (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1500896) | UK multicentre EGDT trial; no significant 90-day mortality advantage and increased treatment costs. | Together with ProCESS/ARISE, supports individualised assessments rather than universally compulsory EGDT. |
| [ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.0071) | 424 patients with septic shock; CRT-guided versus lactate-guided resuscitation. 28-day mortality was 34.9% versus 43.4% (P=.06); not statistically significant for the primary endpoint. | CRT is a meaningful, rapid bedside endpoint; **do not claim this first trial proved a mortality reduction**. Other organ-dysfunction signals were encouraging. |
| [ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.20402) | Multicentre RCT, 1,467 analysed; personalised CRT-directed haemodynamic protocol versus usual care. Hierarchical 28-day primary composite favoured intervention (win ratio **1.16**, 95% CI 1.02–1.33); separate 28-day mortality was **26.5% versus 26.6%**. | Personalising treatment to CRT, diastolic pressure, pulse pressure, fluid responsiveness and echo improves a composite, largely through duration of organ support. It does **not** prove an individual mortality benefit. |
| [SEPSISPAM (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1312173) | Septic shock: MAP target 80–85 versus 65–70 mmHg; no overall survival difference. Higher target increased atrial fibrillation; a prior-hypertension subgroup had less renal-replacement therapy. | MAP ≈65 is a reasonable initial default, not an absolute ceiling or minimum adequate pressure for every patient. Consider chronic hypertension and the clinical response. |
| [65 Trial (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2020.0930) | In older ICU patients with vasodilatory hypotension, permissive hypotension (target MAP 60–65) reduced vasopressor exposure but did not significantly reduce overall 90-day mortality. | A modestly lower pressure may be acceptable in selected older vasodilatory patients with adequate perfusion; avoid generalising to ongoing haemorrhage, acute brain injury or coronary/cerebral hypoperfusion. |

**Why these trials belong together:**

- Rivers taught clinicians to identify shock and treat early
- ProCESS/ARISE/ProMISe demonstrated that rigid invasive algorithms are not mandatory once early standard care improves
- The ANDROMEDA trials emphasise the value of dynamic bedside tissue-perfusion decisions.
- They support the central principle running through Set 1: **treat the mechanism, measure the response, reconsider when the intervention does not improve perfusion**.

## 11.2 The amount and composition of fluid

| **Trial** | **Study and principal result** | **ANZCA Final clinical interpretation** |
|---|---|---|
| [SAFE (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa040232) | Nearly 7,000 Australian/New Zealand ICU patients: 4% albumin versus saline; no overall difference in 28-day mortality. A TBI subgroup generated concern about albumin-containing resuscitation. | Albumin does not confer a general survival benefit over crystalloid for unselected critical illness; consider disease-specific risks, especially brain injury. |
| [6S (2012)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1204242) | Severe sepsis: hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 versus Ringer acetate; higher 90-day mortality (**51% vs 43%**) and more renal-replacement therapy with HES. | **Do not use starches in sepsis**. This complements guideline recommendations against synthetic starch solutions. |
| [SMART (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711584) | Cluster crossover ICU study, 15,802 adults: balanced crystalloid versus saline; MAKE30 **14.3% vs 15.4%**. | Supports balanced crystalloid as a sensible default in many critically ill patients. MAKE30 combines death, new renal-replacement therapy and persistent renal dysfunction; do not describe it simply as a demonstrated mortality reduction. |
| [BaSICS (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2021.11684) | Brazilian multicentre ICU RCT; Plasma-Lyte 148 versus saline showed no significant difference in 90-day mortality (**26.4% vs 27.2%**). | Balanced-versus-saline effects are context-dependent; results of SMART cannot be treated as a universal mortality claim. |
| [PLUS (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114464) | Australasian multicentre ICU RCT: Plasma-Lyte 148 versus saline; 90-day death **21.8% vs 22.0%**, no significant difference. | Highly relevant NZ/Australian evidence: both are acceptable in many ICU situations, though balanced crystalloids remain commonly preferred for large-volume resuscitation and hyperchloraemia concerns. |
| [CLASSIC (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2202707) | ICU septic shock after initial resuscitation: restrictive versus standard fluid, 90-day mortality **42.3% vs 42.1%** (no significant difference). | Avoid claiming restrictive fluid universally improves survival. It supports reassessment and avoiding needless fluid after initial resuscitation. |
| [CLOVERS (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2212663) | Early sepsis-induced hypotension: restrictive-fluid/early-vasopressor versus liberal-fluid strategy; death before discharge up to day 90 **14.0% vs 14.9%**, no significant difference. | Early vasopressor use can be reasonable during selected sepsis resuscitation, but neither strategy proved superior in this population. Do not extrapolate to haemorrhagic shock. |
| [FEAST (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1101549) | Critically ill African children with severe febrile illness, in settings without routine intensive-care support: albumin or saline boluses increased 48-hour mortality compared with no bolus. | Demonstrates that empiric fluid boluses can harm patients in particular contexts. **Do not extrapolate its protocol directly to Australasian paediatric septic shock where full ICU support exists**. |

**Clinical synthesis:**

- Use a suitable crystalloid for a documented indication, reassess its effect on flow and congestion, and stop when benefit is absent or harm develops.
- In uncontrolled major bleeding, select haemostatic blood replacement rather than large-volume crystalloid.
- These trials do not negate the initial-resuscitation guidance in the [2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign](https://sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/surviving-sepsis-campaign-international-guidelines-for-management-of-sepsis-and-septic-shock-2026), which conditionally suggests at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in the first three hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion/shock, with frequent individualised reassessment.

## 11.3 Vasopressors, inotropes, haemorrhage and other high-yield decisions

| **Trial** | **Study and principal result** | **ANZCA Final clinical interpretation** |
|---|---|---|
| [SOAP II (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0907118) | Dopamine versus noradrenaline in shock. Overall 28-day mortality did not significantly differ; arrhythmias were more common with dopamine (**24.1% vs 12.4%**); cardiogenic-shock subgroup suggested harm. | **Noradrenaline is generally preferred** for hypotensive vasodilatory shock. Subgroup mortality signals are not definitive proof of universal survival superiority in cardiogenic shock. |
| [VASST (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa067373) | Low-dose vasopressin plus open-label pressor versus noradrenaline in septic shock; no overall 28-day mortality advantage. | Vasopressin is an **adjunct to reduce catecholamine requirements** when noradrenaline alone is inadequate, not a universally superior first-line vasopressor. |
| [VANISH (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2016.10485) | Vasopressin versus noradrenaline and hydrocortisone versus placebo in septic shock; primary kidney-failure-free days were not significantly different overall. | No mandate to replace noradrenaline with vasopressin as first line. Steroids and vasopressin have context-dependent roles in refractory shock. |
| [ATHOS-3 (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1704154) | Angiotensin II in catecholamine-resistant vasodilatory shock increased achievement of target MAP over three hours compared with placebo. | An option in **selected refractory vasoplegia**, with thromboembolic risk and specialist oversight. **BP-response efficacy is not proof of improved survival**. |
| [ADRENAL (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1705835) | Australasian-led septic shock RCT: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day versus placebo; no significant 90-day mortality difference, but more rapid shock resolution. | Hydrocortisone is reasonable in selected patients requiring ongoing significant vasopressor support; discuss haemodynamic rather than proven mortality benefit. |
| [APROCCHSS (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1705716) | Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone versus placebo in septic shock; lower 90-day mortality in this population. | Benefits vary with steroid regimen and illness severity; do not assume all steroid trials are interchangeable. |
| [CRASH-2 (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2810%2960835-5) | Randomised trauma trial of early TXA in patients with significant bleeding/risk; reduced bleeding-related death, with timing crucial. | Give indicated TXA **early, within 3 h of injury**, following trauma protocol. Later administration may not help and can harm; it does not substitute for definitive haemostasis. |
| [PROPPR (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.12) | Major trauma: plasma:platelet:RBC 1:1:1 versus 1:1:2; no statistically significant difference in overall 24-hour or 30-day mortality, but more haemostasis and fewer early exsanguination deaths in 1:1:1 group. | Supports organised early balanced component delivery in massive transfusion, followed by **laboratory- and viscoelastic-guided individualisation**, rather than claiming 1:1:1 proved a universal mortality benefit. |
| [POISE-3 blood-pressure strategy (2023)](https://doi.org/10.7326/M22-3157) | Two bundled perioperative strategies in hypertensive patients (higher MAP goal plus withheld medicines versus lower MAP goal plus continuation); no significant reduction in major vascular outcomes. | Does not validate a mandatory “within 20% of baseline” rule, nor identify one independent ideal BP target. Patient and procedure remain decisive. |

## 11.4 Critical appraisal: three recurring examination mistakes

- **1.** **A nonsignificant primary outcome is not equivalence.** CLASSIC, CLOVERS and several haemodynamic strategy trials have clinically important confidence intervals; they demonstrate that a difference was not established in the studied context, not that approaches are universally interchangeable.
- **2.** **A composite outcome is not the same as survival.** ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 improved a hierarchical outcome, much of the signal related to time requiring organ support; its separate mortality comparison was neutral. SMART's MAKE30 is a renal composite, not standalone kidney-failure or survival proof.
- **3.** **Physiological plausibility does not establish benefit.** Raising MAP, increasing cardiac index or correcting lactate by any means can worsen the patient when the intervention raises afterload, worsens congestion or treats a marker rather than the cause.
  - Mention the study's intervention, population, outcome and limitations before using it in a viva.

items.title: Reading pathway and linked references
items.body:
- The sources below are ordered for a **teaching sequence**, not merely alphabetically.
- Primary guidelines govern current recommendations; BJA Education helps explain the underlying physiology; the Blue Book and ANZCA examiner reports add relevant Australasian and examination context.
- For textbooks, sections are identified as recommended reading rather than asserting that a full paywalled edition was directly accessible.

## 12.1 Essential BJA Education reading

| **Resource** | **Why read it alongside these notes** |
|---|---|
| [Jha A et al. Vasoactive therapy in shock (2021), BJA Education](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8212163/) | **Chapters 1, 6 and 7.** Mechanism-driven selection of vasopressor, inotrope and inodilator; sympathetic physiology, drug adverse effects, distributive versus cardiogenic shock. |
| [Madhivathanan PR et al. Perioperative implications of pericardial effusions and cardiac tamponade (2020), BJA Education](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7808091/) | **Chapter 8.** Pericardial compliance, echo signs, induction dangers and drainage planning; combine with newer ESC 2025 pericardial guidance and ANZCOR traumatic-arrest guidance. |
| [Ilyas C et al. ## 12.3 Contemporary clinical guidance

- **1.** [2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-026-08361-1)**.** Antibiotic and source-control timing
  - Early fluid treatment with individualisation
  - Dynamic fluid tests, CRT/lactate trends, vasopressors, inotropes and steroids.
  - In all areas, distinguish conditional from strong recommendations.
- **2.** [ESICM 2025: Circulatory shock and haemodynamic monitoring](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00134-025-08137-z)**.** Assessment of shock phenotype, echocardiography, dynamic fluid responsiveness, reassessment and haemodynamic endpoints.
- **3.** [ESICM 2025: Fluid therapy in acute circulatory failure](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40163133/)**.** Disease-specific fluid therapy rather than universal bolus volumes, including when fluid is unsafe in cardiac and obstructive disorders.
- **4.** [POQI consensus on perioperative arterial pressure management (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11282474/)**.** Clinical harm of sustained hypotension; appropriate but individualised monitoring and treatment targets.
- **5.** [2026 Association of Anaesthetists / BIHS perioperative blood-pressure guidance](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.70082)**.** Preoperative thresholds and perioperative hypertension/medication management, including differences from ACC/AHA approaches.
- **6.** [ESC 2025 Guidelines for pericardial diseases](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192)**.** Drainage strategy, image guidance, haemorrhagic tamponade, loculated effusions, complications and postoperative care.
- **7.** [ANZCOR traumatic cardiac arrest (2026), Guideline 11.10.1](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-1-management-of-cardiac-arrest-due-to-trauma)**.** Reversible obstructive causes and the importance of surgical intervention in traumatic tamponade; do not treat needle aspiration as routinely definitive.
- **8.** [AO Spine/Praxis acute spinal cord injury haemodynamic guideline (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10964888/)**.** Specific MAP augmentation goals for acute spinal injury; not general shock or post-neuraxial hypotension targets.
- **9.** [Perioperative Quality Initiative: intraoperative goal-directed haemodynamic therapy consensus (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.05.033)**.** Individualised haemodynamic optimisation and the limitations of applying a standard algorithm to every unstable patient.

NICE CG174 (IV fluids in adults): [Replacement and redistribution of existing fluid/electrolyte deficits and ongoing losses](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg174/chapter/Recommendations); separate from maintenance and emergency resuscitation.

NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: [Traumatic haemorrhagic shock quick reference](https://aci.health.nsw.gov.au/networks/trauma/resources/traumatic-haemorrhagic-shock); traditional ATLS class comparison, not a validated blood-loss estimator.

ACC/AHA perioperative cardiovascular guidance (2024): [Intraoperative MAP 60–65 mmHg/SBP 90 mmHg minimum and postoperative hypotension treatment](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.06.013); compare with the higher-risk targets noted by Association of Anaesthetists/BIHS 2026.

## 12.4 Suggested authoritative textbook chapters

- **Miller's Anesthesia:** cardiovascular physiology and monitoring, perioperative fluid therapy, haemorrhage/transfusion, and cardiovascular complications. Use for mechanism detail and anaesthesia-specific implications.
- **Yao & Artusio's Anesthesiology: Problem-Oriented Patient Management:** hypotension/shock, emergency and trauma scenarios. Use to rehearse how a candidate explains a decision aloud.
- **Marino's The ICU Book and **Oh's Intensive Care Manual:**** shock phenotypes, haemodynamic monitoring, acute circulatory failure and vasoactive pharmacology; cross-check numerical recommendations with the current guidelines above.
- **ATLS principles:** haemorrhage recognition and source-control priorities; interpret traditional classes as teaching patterns, not a validated volume estimate for individuals.
